framing: Capacity you can use before the deadline passes
paragraphs: On a web fleet, you can often react to load. A GPU worker can take minutes to become useful, so the new replica may arrive after the burst that asked for it has given up. That one fact shapes nearly every decision in this chapter.

Running a fleet here means running two loops on different clocks: one that handles requests now and one that changes what you'll have later. The engineering is in being honest about the gap, by measuring readiness, pricing warm capacity, and rejecting work you can't serve before it times out.

We'll work through one morning surge with real arithmetic: how much fits on a card, how many replicas a benchmark implies, how many requests make their deadline with one warm worker or three, and where a cold start spends its time.
Then we'll take on the messy parts: probes that restart the wrong thing, retries that amplify an outage, spot instances with a short warning, and three different ways a spike can stall.
outcomes: Size a worker's memory, and turn a measured capacity point into a replica target.
Work out which requests of a burst make their deadline, and what warm capacity that takes.
Set up readiness, queue gating, and drain so overload fails fast and recovers cleanly.
question: Max replicas is set to 20, so the plan covers the traffic on paper. What has to be true for the first 100 requests to be served?
